items.item: The named trade-off: simpler code, better scalability, lower latency, and more flexibility gained by this approach.

An engine choice rests on three drivers — state size, the latency floor the data-flow shape already set, and whether the team can operate it — with the last one counted as a real cost, not an afterthought.

items.item: The amplification ledger compares designs by physical bytes moved (after replication, rewrite and compaction), never by logical volume alone.
A design that looks cheapest by its logical size can have the largest amplification factor once a full rewrite or heavy compaction is counted honestly.

This topic leaves out engine internals (Chapters 2, 7, 9) and serving-store internals (Chapter 5, Chapter 6 §6.4, Chapter 9, Chapter 17) deliberately — it teaches the decision those mechanics execute, not the mechanics themselves.

The single-node renaissance (DuckDB, Polars) is the one still-growing option in this topic, as capacity estimates increasingly justify skipping a distributed engine for workloads that fit on one machine.
A fix that computes a new breakdown on demand (the clustering-key option) survives a changed question untouched; a fixed-shape pre-aggregate usually needs a full rebuild.
This topic fixes the shop's own engine and serving-store choices that the next topic (correctness under replay and late data) assumes already hold on a normal day.
